slides.text:
Own-Price Elasticity and Total Revenue
Elastic
Increase (a decrease) in price leads to a decrease (an increase) in total revenue.
Inelastic
Increase (a decrease) in price leads to an increase (a decrease) in total revenue.
Unitary
Total revenue is maximized at the point where demand is unitary elastic.

slides.title: Factors Affecting Own Price Elasticity
slides.text:
Factors Affecting Own Price Elasticity
Available Substitutes
The more substitutes available for the good, the more elastic the demand.
Time
Demand tends to be more inelastic in the short term than in the long term.
Time allows consumers to seek out available substitutes.
Expenditure Share
Goods that comprise a small share of consumer’s budgets tend to be more inelastic than goods for which consumers spend a large portion of their incomes.

slides.title: Question
slides.text:
Question
The inverse demand curve for a firm's product is given by:
P = 16 − 2Q
How much would the firm's revenue change if it lowered the price from $12 to $8? Is demand elastic or inelastic in this range?
How much would the firm's revenue change if it lowered the price from $4 to $2? Is demand elastic or inelastic in this range?

bullets.text: The inverse demand curve for a firm's product is given by:

How much would the firm's revenue change if it lowered the price from $4 to $2? Is demand elastic or inelastic in this range?

slides.title: Demand function: Q = 8 − 0.5P
slides.text:
Demand function: Q = 8 − 0.5P
At P=$12: Q = 8 − 6 = 2, TR = 12 × 2 = $24
At P=$8: Q = 8 − 4 = 4, TR = 8 × 4 = $32
Revenue rises by $8 as price falls → demand is elastic in this range.
At P=$4: Q = 8 − 2 = 6, TR = 4 × 6 = $24
At P=$2: Q = 8 − 1 = 7, TR = 2 × 7 = $14
Revenue falls by $10 as price falls → demand is inelastic in this range.

bullets.text: Revenue rises by $8 as price falls → demand is elastic in this range.
Revenue falls by $10 as price falls → demand is inelastic in this range.

Income increases by 6 percent.

slides.title: Practice Question
slides.text:
Practice Question
You are the manager of a firm that receives revenues of $50,000 per year from product A and $120,000 per year from product B. The own-price elasticity of demand for product A is −1.2, and the cross-price elasticity of demand between product B and product A is −2.5.
How will your firm's total revenue (revenues from both products) change if you increase the price of product A by 3 percent?

slides.title: Example 1: Pricing and Cash Flows
slides.text:
Example 1: Pricing and Cash Flows
According to an FTC Report by Michael Ward, AT&T’s own price elasticity of demand for long distance services is -8.64.
AT&T needs to boost revenues in order to meet it’s marketing goals.
To accomplish this goal, should AT&T raise or lower it’s price?
Michael R. Baye, Managerial Economics and Business Strategy, 6e. ©The McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc., 2008

slides.title: Answer: Lower price!
slides.text:
Answer: Lower price!
Since demand is elastic, a reduction in price will increase quantity demanded by a greater percentage than the price decline, resulting in more revenues for AT&T.
Michael R. Baye, Managerial Economics and Business Strategy, 6e. ©The McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc., 2008

slides.text:
Interpreting the Regression Output
The estimated log-linear demand function is:
ln(Qx) = 7.58 - 0.84 ln(Px).
Own price elasticity: -0.84 (inelastic).
How good is our estimate?
t-statistics of 5.29 and -2.80 indicate that the estimated coefficients are statistically different from zero.
R-square of 0.17 indicates the ln(PX) variable explains only 17 percent of the variation in ln(Qx).
F-statistic significant at the 1 percent level.

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.text:
Conclusion
Elasticities are tools you can use to quantify the impact of changes in prices, income, and advertising on sales and revenues.
Given market or survey data, regression analysis can be used to estimate:
Demand functions.
Elasticities.
A host of other things, including cost functions.
Managers can quantify the impact of changes in prices, income, advertising, etc.
